A self-directed quantitative finance research project

What happens
when an idea
meets the market?

I am building this lab to apply my software engineering, machine learning, statistics, and data systems background to questions in quantitative finance. Its strategy lab tests simple rules against historical prices and asks what the evidence can—and cannot—support. A separate options calculator examines theoretical prices under stated assumptions.

01 THE IDEA

A time machine
for a trading rule.

A backtest asks: “What would have happened if I had followed this rule in the past?”

You choose a period, a starting amount of imaginary money, and a rule. The lab walks through historical prices in order, simulates buying or selling, and tracks the portfolio’s value.

Quantitative research simply means using numbers and repeatable rules to investigate an idea. Here, you can inspect the decisions, compare the outcome, and keep a record of what you tested.

WHY I BUILT THIS

My background is primarily in computer science and software engineering. I built Orion to develop the mathematical, statistical, and financial research skills that quantitative finance requires, through small experiments I can explain and repeat.

KEEP THIS IN MIND

This is a historical simulation. No money is deposited, no brokerage is connected, and no real trades are placed. A successful trip through the past cannot tell you what happens next.

02 THE RULES

Three ways to travel
through the same history.

The lab starts with SPY, an exchange-traded fund: a basket of investments that trades like a stock. SPY tracks the S&P 500, an index of large U.S. companies.

RULE A / THE REFERENCE POINT

Buy and hold.

Buy at the first selected closing price. Keep the investment until the experiment ends.

“What if I simply stayed invested?”

This is the benchmark—the simple alternative your idea is compared against. It receives the same starting capital, dates, asset, and cost assumptions.

RULE B / THE QUESTION

Follow the momentum.

Own the asset when its previous closing price is higher than its close a chosen number of sessions earlier. Otherwise, hold cash.

“Does a recent rise tend to continue?”

The lookback is that number of trading sessions. A 30-day lookback means 30 market observations, not 30 calendar days. This rule can miss recoveries or trade repeatedly in a choppy market.

RULE C / A DIFFERENT TREND TEST

Compare with the recent average.

The moving-average filter owns the asset when yesterday’s close is strictly above the average of the previous N closes, including yesterday. Otherwise it holds cash. The decision uses only earlier prices and takes effect at today’s close.

“Is the latest close above its recent trend?”

This gives a second, testable definition of a trend. It shares the same asset, benchmark, transaction-cost setting, and limitations as the momentum rule.

You can also import your own daily CSV. The benchmark then holds that same imported asset, rather than SPY.

03 THE MACHINERY

The past arrives
one day at a time.

The engine must only use information that was already available. Seeing tomorrow’s price today would make the experiment unfair.

  1. OBSERVE

    Read yesterday’s prices.

    Momentum compares yesterday’s close with one lookback earlier; the moving-average filter compares it with a recent average. Earlier data warms up either rule before your selected test window.

  2. DECIDE

    Trade at today’s close.

    If the rule changes from cash to invested, buy. If it changes back, sell. Deduct the selected fee and adverse execution slippage on each transaction.

  3. MEASURE

    Count what happens next.

    A purchase at today’s close first earns the return from today to tomorrow. Each day’s cash plus investment value becomes a point on the chart.

From hypothesis to a credible result

IN THE LAB TODAY
  1. State a hypothesis and choose a historical window before changing the rule.
  2. Prepare daily adjusted prices or validate an imported CSV.
  3. Implement the rule without using future prices, then run the backtest.
  4. Compare with buy and hold under the same dates, capital, and modeled trade costs.
  5. Examine returns, volatility, drawdown, Sharpe ratio, and the trade record.
VALIDATION IN THE LAB
  1. Reserve unseen data for out-of-sample and walk-forward testing.
  2. Disclose the breadth of training-only parameter comparisons.
  3. Test fee sensitivity and model execution slippage separately.
A small example: why timing matters

Suppose Monday closes at $100 and Tuesday at $110. A one-session momentum rule sees that rise and buys at Wednesday’s close. It cannot claim the gain from Monday to Tuesday—or any movement earlier on Wednesday—because it did not own the asset then.

Where the history comes from

Daily SPY prices come from Yahoo Finance. A weekday refresh is scheduled for 23:30 UTC: 7:30 p.m. Eastern in summer and 6:30 p.m. in winter. Today’s prices are excluded until 6 p.m. Eastern. The lab displays the latest available date and warns when data is old.

Prices are adjusted for dividends and stock splits so comparisons use a consistent basis. They are research values, not the exact historical prices at which you could have traded.

What the model assumes

You can own fractional units or hold cash. Cash earns no interest. The model has no borrowing, taxes, or separate estimate for the difference between expected and actual trade prices. Open holdings are valued at the final close without a forced sale.

Calculations run in your browser. The data source is unofficial; a failed refresh keeps the last published dataset available. “Check for data update” checks that published snapshot, not live quotes.

04 THE EVIDENCE

Read the journey.
Not just the finish.

The portfolio chart shows how your imaginary money changed over time. The solid line follows your rule; the dashed line follows buy and hold.

Total return
How much did the portfolio gain or lose?

Starting with $100 and ending with $120 means a 20% return. The lab includes modeled trading costs.

Maximum drawdown
How far did it fall from an earlier peak?

If the portfolio reaches $120, then falls to $90, that decline is 25%. A later recovery does not erase the experience of that fall.

Volatility
How uneven was the ride?

This measures the variation in daily returns, scaled to a year. It counts both upward and downward movement; it is not a worst-case loss.

Sharpe ratio
How much return came with that variation?

This compares average daily return with daily volatility, scaled to a year. Here the cash reference rate is zero. Higher values indicate more return per unit of variation in this sample, not a guarantee of a better strategy.

For the curious: the calculations

Total return = final value ÷ starting capital − 1. Volatility = sample standard deviation of daily returns × √252. Sharpe = mean daily return ÷ that daily standard deviation × √252. The lab assumes 252 trading sessions per year and reports Sharpe as N/A when variation is zero. Drawdown compares each value with the highest value reached so far, including starting capital.

A RESEARCHER’S CAUTION

Trying many settings and keeping only the winner can fit the quirks of the past. This is called overfitting. The lab can rank a small, disclosed set of lookbacks on training data, then report performance on a separate, untouched test period. Use a good result as a reason to ask more questions.

05 YOUR FIRST EXPERIMENT

Begin with a question.
Leave with evidence.

Try this: “How does a 30-session momentum rule compare with simply holding SPY?”

  1. Keep SPY and choose momentum.

    Use the default dataset and “Time-series momentum.” Start with a lookback of 30. For your first run, the default dates provide enough earlier history to warm up the rule.

  2. Set the terms of the experiment.

    Start with $100,000 of simulated capital and 5 basis points per trade. A basis point is 0.01%, so 5 bps means a $5 cost for every $10,000 bought or sold.

  3. Run it. Look at both lines.

    Click “Run backtest.” Compare return and drawdown with the benchmark. Then inspect Trade history to see when the rule bought, sold, or stayed in cash.

  4. Change one thing and ask why.

    Try a 60-session lookback, keeping everything else the same. Did trading become less frequent? Did the portfolio miss a recovery? Changing one setting makes the comparison easier to understand.

  5. Keep your evidence.

    “Save experiment” keeps a run in this browser on this device, up to the latest 10. “Export experiment JSON” downloads the data, settings, and results. “Export equity CSV” downloads daily values you can open in a spreadsheet. Clearing browser storage removes local saves.

Bring your own dataset

Choose “Import daily CSV,” enter an asset label, and select a file with date,close columns. Use dates like 2026-01-02, positive decimal prices, and one row per daily observation, oldest first. Dates must be unique. Use a consistent adjustment basis and include enough observations before your start date for the momentum lookback.

The lab accepts 3–20,000 rows in a file smaller than 2 MB. It validates the format but cannot independently verify your provider’s prices or trading calendar.

06 RESEARCH RECORD

What is built.
What comes next.

Orion is a working learning project, not a record of live trading. Its current scope is deliberately narrow so that each calculation and assumption can be inspected.

WORKING NOW

Historical experiments

  • SPY daily adjusted-price snapshot and validated daily CSV import.
  • Time-series momentum, moving-average trend filter, and buy-and-hold backtests with configurable dates, capital, lookback, and proportional trade costs.
  • Same-asset benchmark; equity and drawdown charts; return, annualized return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown.
  • Trade history, browser-local saved experiments, and JSON or equity CSV exports.
  • A separate Black–Scholes–Merton options pricer ↗ for theoretical European values, Greeks, and hypothetical spot scenarios.
PLANNED RESEARCH

Stronger tests and broader models

  • Training-only parameter comparison, fixed train/test separation, and expanding walk-forward validation.
  • Transaction-cost sensitivity across disclosed fixed assumptions.
  • Independent fee-and-slippage sensitivity scenarios.
  • Only after the validation foundation: factor research, portfolio optimization, Monte Carlo methods, and historical options research when suitable data exists.
ONE REPRODUCIBLE OBSERVATION

On the bundled SPY snapshot ending October 1, 2026, a 30-session moving-average filter from January 4, 2021 returned 37.32% after modeled 5-bps trade costs, versus 123.55% for buy and hold. Its maximum drawdown was smaller (17.29% versus 24.50%), but it made 134 trades and incurred $7,768 in modeled costs on $100,000 of starting capital. This is one in-sample result, not evidence of future performance; later data refreshes may change it.

IMPLEMENTED ARCHITECTURE

A static HTML/CSS and browser JavaScript interface runs separate JavaScript backtest and options-pricing engines. Python scripts validate and refresh the published daily dataset. GitHub Actions checks the lab; the portfolio's scheduled workflow refreshes the published data. The portfolio serves the reviewed lab build from a Dockerized Nginx site.

The current code does not use a server API, database, React, or a machine-learning model. Those would be separate future design decisions, not existing capabilities.

RESEARCH PRINCIPLE

Historical backtests do not imply future profitability. This lab is for learning quantitative modeling, statistical reasoning, numerical experimentation, and financial-market behavior—not for trading real money.

THE NEXT EXHIBIT IS YOURS

You have the question.
Now run the experiment.

The lab is a place to learn how an idea behaves—and where it breaks.
